conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having severe abdominal pain since last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's sharp and in my upper belly, left of center. It gets worse when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you haven't passed gas or had a bowel movement since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing. That’s really unusual for me. I usually have many loose stools every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of sclerosing mesenteritis and multiple bowel obstructions, this could be another partial blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels just like my past obstructions. Is that what the X-ray showed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels, which suggests ileus or partial obstruction. But stool is still moving into your rectum, so it’s not a complete blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. We’ll insert a nasogastric tube to decompress your stomach and bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s uncomfortable, but I know it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also start IV fluids and give you pain and nausea meds. Your labs show low calcium and magnesium, so we’ll replace those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’m just glad it’s not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your NG tube drained about 460 mL yesterday, and you had three bowel movements. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. Is the blockage clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like it. We’ll try clamping the NG tube today to see if you can tolerate it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start drinking water if it goes well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with a clear liquid diet if you don’t have nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed the clamp trial. We’re removing the NG tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. I hated that tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on clear liquids and will advance to full liquids, then soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my IV? It’s been hard to keep it in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a PICC line placement today for better access, since you’ve had trouble in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Is it done with ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and fluoroscopy to guide it. It’ll go into your right arm and end in a large vein near your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully in your right axillary vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my arm is burning—sharp pain from shoulder to hand. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted neurology. They think it’s nerve irritation from the line placement, not damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away? Shouldn’t they pull the line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They don’t think removing it will help. It should improve with time. We’ll start a lidocaine patch and increase your gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust them. Just want the pain to ease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also advancing you to a regular diet today. You’ve been stooling regularly, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate toast and applesauce earlier—no nausea. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. Your labs are stable—hemoglobin is 9.0, and electrolytes are normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still low hemoglobin, but I’ve always been anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic anemia from your bowel issues. We’re not concerned as long as it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is controlled, you’re eating regular food, and your arm pain is improving with the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been walking the halls too. Feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual meds. We’re increasing gabapentin to 1200 mg twice daily for your arm nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lidocaine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one patch daily on your right arm as needed. We’re also switching from pantoprazole to famotidine for stomach protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my liver history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, and famotidine is safer long-term. You’ll keep taking rivaroxaban for your DVT history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—no NSAIDs, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stick to acetaminophen or your prescribed oxycodone for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your bowel function has returned, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have increasing pain, vomiting, or can’t pass stool or gas. Also, monitor your arm for worsening pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with Dr. ___ as planned. Take care, and we’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.
